hints.title: Draw the common region
hints.body: Rearrange both inequalities to put y on its own. Sketch the line and the parabola, then shade where both inequalities hold.
hints.recap: A point belongs to an intersection of regions only if it satisfies every defining inequality.
hints.pitfall: The boundary curves are excluded because the inequalities are strict.
hints.pause: Use the shared shaded region to test statement I.

recall.reminder: A point belongs to an intersection of regions only if it satisfies every defining inequality.

hints.title: Simplify the product
hints.body: For II, start by setting x to zero. Work out which y-values lie in the region and what the proposed product becomes.
hints.recap: Before multiplying inequalities, check the signs of the quantities involved.
hints.pitfall: Multiplying two upper bounds is unsafe when the factors can be negative.
hints.pause: Find whether the product inequality holds for every allowed y.

recall.reminder: Before multiplying inequalities, check the signs of the quantities involved.

hints.title: Test the proposed height limit
hints.body: For III, try points on the line y=x. Substitute into both region inequalities before checking the proposed upper bound on y.
hints.recap: One valid counterexample disproves a statement that is claimed for every point.
hints.pitfall: A point that fails either region inequality cannot be used as a counterexample.
hints.pause: Choose suitable points, check them and decide which statements always hold.

recall.reminder: One valid counterexample disproves a statement that is claimed for every point.

solution:
I fails at (10, 0): 0−10<3 and 0−100<1, but x=10 is outside(−1, 2).

II fails at (0, −2): both premises hold, while(y−x)(y−x2)=(−2)(−2)=4, not less than 3.

III fails at (6, 6): 6−6=0<3 and 6−36=−30<1, but y=6 is not less than 5.

Each example obeys both premises, so none of I–III holds for every point: A.
